results.summary: This project implements a 4-bit ripple carry adder without carry-in, taking two 4-bit inputs A and B and producing a 5-bit sum output. It is used by applying logic levels to the eight input pins and observing the five output pins, for example with a scope. External hardware can include LEDs with series resistors on the outputs and switches on the inputs to make testing easier. The design is a simple educational arithmetic block built in Wokwi, and the documentation is brief but sufficient to describe its function.

This is an unmodified Tiny Tapeout Wokwi template with two input pins and one output pin, and its documentation still contains placeholder text. No actual logic function is described beyond the template structure. It is intended as a starting point for a user to fill in their own design and test instructions. Because the documentation is essentially empty, no specific behavior or external hardware can be determined.

This design is a small combinational circuit made of NOT gates and an AND gate, with eight inputs and eight outputs. It is tested by flipping input switches until the outputs show a pattern that looks like the digit 8. The author is unsure what external hardware is needed, though switches and some display would be typical. It appears to be a beginner Wokwi exercise, and the documentation is very thin about the exact logic mapping.

This project accepts an 8-bit input code and displays the letter A on a 7-segment display when the correct secret code is entered. It is tested by trying different input combinations to guess the secret code. No external hardware is required according to the documentation. The design is a simple Wokwi workshop exercise, and the documentation does not reveal the secret code or the exact comparison logic.

This design takes a 3-bit input value and displays it on a 7-segment display through seven segment output pins. It is tested by applying different 3-bit input values and checking that the corresponding digit appears. A 7-segment display is the required external hardware. The project is a straightforward Wokwi exercise in binary-to-seven-segment decoding, though the documentation is minimal.

This Verilog design echoes a predefined text string onto a 16x2 character LCD using a 4-bit data interface with RS and E control signals. It is used by connecting an LCD1602 module according to the pinout and supplying a clock on the input pin. The only external hardware needed is the 16x2 character LCD. The project is notable for fitting an LCD text controller into a single Tiny Tapeout tile, though the documentation is very brief.

This project shares the title and description of another LCD text design but has a different pinout with eight generic inputs and one output, and its one-line description says the design is not yet decided. The documentation claims it echoes predefined text onto a 16x2 character LCD, but the pin names do not match that function. It would be tested by connecting an LCD1602 and setting the clock, yet the pin mapping makes this unclear. The documentation is contradictory and too thin to determine the actual behavior.

This design displays symbols on a 7-segment LED display based on an 8-bit input binary word, and it outputs the letter n only when the input equals 0b00010101. It is tested by trying different input words and verifying that outputs 0, 1, 2, 4, and 5 are high only for that specific input. External hardware includes eight input switches and a 7-segment LED display. The project is a simple Wokwi exercise in binary pattern detection and seven-segment output, with clear but limited documentation.

This project is described as an adder with three input pins and two output pins, but the documentation says it works by magic and gives no real explanation. It is tested simply by using it, with switches and LED displays listed as external hardware. No details are provided about the bit width, encoding, or internal logic of the adder. The documentation is too thin to determine the actual behavior beyond the title.

This design combines four basic building blocks: an inverter, an AND gate, an OR gate, and an Earle latch with an enable signal, mapped across several input and output pins. It is tested by exercising every input combination for the NOT, AND, and OR gates and by checking that the latch holds both a 0 and a 1. No external addons are required. The project is an educational Wokwi exercise in fundamental digital logic, and the documentation describes the intended connections clearly.
